rows.evidence: Q1: Sections 2.1-2.3 and Tables 1-3 report a two-year randomized block field experiment (seven replications) on broccoli and cauliflower in Nadia, West Bengal, comparing surface irrigation with gravity drip and micro-sprinkler irrigation at 1.0 and 0.7 of pan evaporation, with measured As content, yield, water use and water productivity.
rows.notes: The study is a primary field trial, but it tests gravity-fed drip and micro-sprinkler irrigation scheduled by pan-evaporation replenishment, not app-based or 'smart' irrigation scheduling; no app, sensor-based controller or decision-support tool is involved. The claimed effect (risk management / climate adaptation) is also not what the study measures: its own results are reduced arsenic accumulation in edible heads (6.78-16.6%), reduced antioxidant enzyme activity, reduced dietary carcinogenic risk (SAMOE), higher head yield at 1.0 E0, water saving up to 37.3% and higher benefit-cost ratio for drip at 1.0 ETc. Water saving is reported, but it is attributed to micro-irrigation hardware, not to app scheduling, and is not framed as climate resilience. Hence Q2 is no for technology (and effect) mismatch.

notes: Full text available and complete. Single-site (one village, one soil), two crops, two years; the authors themselves note the need for up-scaling to diverse physiographic locations and that applicability to rice is hindered. None of this bears on the app-scheduling claim because the technology differs.
